Paszto
PAHSH-toh
n. (the Hungarian Cistercian abbey of 1190, formerly Benedictine, keeping a medieval glassworks and school)
Hungarian Paszto, probably from pasztor, a shepherd, or a personal name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Paszto in northern Hungary was a Benedictine house that passed to the Cistercians in 1190, settled from Pilis, and it is unusual among Hungarian abbeys for what the excavations found: a medieval glassworks with furnaces and crucibles, and the foundations of a school building, both inside the monastic precinct. The abbey ran a mill on the Zagyva and kept vineyards on the hillside. It was ruined in the Ottoman wars and partly rebuilt in the eighteenth century. The dictionary records Paszto for its workshops, because a monastery with a furnace in the yard is a standing argument against the division of life into sacred and secular hours. Work is the ordinary appointment of fallen man and is nowhere treated as beneath him, “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Gen 3:19), and the apostolic rule for a community of believers is bluntly practical, “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10). The proverb promises a return and contrasts it with talk, “In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23). What Scripture does question is spending on what does not feed, “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” (Isa 55:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a crucible as a melting pot for metals; a furnace as a place where a vehement fire is maintained; a mill as a machine for grinding; a vineyard as a plantation of vines; and penury as want, extreme poverty.

expand to see more

CRUCIBLE, n. A melting pot, made of earth, and used by chemists and others for melting metals.

FURNACE, n. A place where a vehement fire and heat may be made and maintained, for melting ores or other substances.

MILL, n. A complicated engine or machine for grinding and reducing to fine particles, grain, fruit or other substance.

VINEYARD, n. A plantation of vines producing grapes; an inclosure devoted to the culture of grapes.

PENURY, n. Want of property; indigence; extreme poverty.

Key Scripture

Gen 3:19 — "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return."

2Th 3:10 — "For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat."

Pro 14:23 — "In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury."

Isa 55:2 — "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness."

Modern Corruption

Hungarian Cistercian abbey of 1190 with a medieval glassworks, a school, a mill and vineyards inside the precinct.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a furnace in a monastic yard refutes the division of hours into sacred and secular. Paszto blew glass and ground corn beside its choir, and work is presented in Scripture as the common appointment of men rather than a lower calling, “till thou return unto the ground” (Gen 3:19).

The live temptation runs both ways, toward a contemplation that despises the forge and toward an industry that forgets why it was lit. The apostolic rule settles the first, “this we commanded you” (2Th 3:10); the proverb promises the forge a return and gives idle talk none, “but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23); and the prophet questions not the labour but its object, “and your labour for that which satisfieth not?” (Isa 55:2).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew abad (H5647), to labour; Greek ergazomai (G2038), to work; Hebrew mothar (H4195), profit; Hebrew sabea (H7646), to be satisfied.

expand to see more

Hebrew abad (H5647) — to labour, to till, to serve; “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread”, Genesis 3:19.

Greek ergazomai (G2038) — to work, to labour; “if any would not work”, 2 Thessalonians 3:10.

Hebrew mothar (H4195) — profit, that which remains over; “In all labour there is profit”, Proverbs 14:23.

Hebrew machsor (H4270) — want, need, penury; “tendeth only to penury”, Proverbs 14:23.

Hebrew sabea (H7646) — to be sated, to be satisfied; “for that which satisfieth not?”, Isaiah 55:2.

Usage

"“In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Gen 3:19) — work as the common appointment."

"“if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10) — the apostolic rule for a community."

"“Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” (Isa 55:2) — the object questioned, not the labour."
